introduction-the-layers-of-the-edge.core: CloudFront's edge is layered: hundreds of edge locations close to users, regional edge caches with larger capacity behind them, optional Origin Shield as a single caching layer in front of the origin, and the origin itself. Each layer absorbs requests so fewer reach the next, improving latency and protecting origins.

first_principles.problem: Origin servers are overwhelmed by cache misses from hundreds of edge locations.

analogy.title: Neighbourhood shops, regional warehouses and the factory
analogy.story: Most shoppers are served locally; only rare items go back to the factory.
analogy.breaks: Shops restock on schedule; caches fill on demand.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: One origin fetch serves the world.

check.q: What sits between edge locations and Origin Shield?

origin-shield-the-super-cache.core: Origin Shield is an optional extra caching layer in one chosen region in front of your origin. All regional edge caches route misses through it, so concurrent requests for the same object collapse into one origin fetch, raising cache hit ratio, reducing origin load and egress, and helping multi-CDN or live-streaming setups.

first_principles.problem: A video launch causes hundreds of simultaneous origin requests for the same segments from different regions.
derivation: Enable **Origin Shield** in the region **closest to the origin**.
Benefit most for **global audiences**, **live video**, **expensive origins**.

analogy.title: A single wholesaler buying for all regional shops
analogy.story: Instead of every shop calling the factory, one buyer places one order.
analogy.breaks: Wholesalers add markup; Shield adds a small per-request fee.

check.q: Where should you place Origin Shield?
check.a: In the AWS region closest to (or hosting) your origin.

compute-at-the-edge-lambdaedge-vs-cloudf.core: CloudFront Functions are lightweight JavaScript running at every edge location for viewer request/response events, with sub-ms execution and very low cost, good for header manipulation, redirects, URL rewrites and simple auth. Lambda@Edge runs Node/Python at regional edge caches on all four events (including origin request/response), with network access and more time, for heavier logic.

first_principles.problem: A team uses Lambda@Edge for simple header rewrites, paying more and adding latency.
truths: Heavier logic needs network and longer runtime.
Running closer to viewers is faster.
derivation: **CloudFront Functions** for viewer events: headers, redirects, rewrites, token checks.
**Lambda@Edge** for origin events, network calls, larger payloads.

analogy.title: A doorman versus a concierge desk
analogy.story: The doorman handles quick tasks instantly at every door; the concierge handles complex requests from a few desks.
analogy.breaks: Doormen can make calls; CloudFront Functions have no network access.

example.title: URL rewrite

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Static site routing at near-zero cost.

example.outcome: edge logic at the right tier.

check.q: Which edge compute option can run on origin request events?
check.a: Lambda@Edge (CloudFront Functions only run on viewer events).

securing-content-signed-urls-vs-signed-c.core: Signed URLs and signed cookies restrict CloudFront content to authorised users, using a key group's private key to sign policies with expiry, IP ranges or path wildcards. Signed URLs suit individual files; signed cookies suit many files (HLS segments, a member area) without changing URLs. Origin access control keeps S3 private behind CloudFront.

first_principles.problem: Premium videos are downloadable by anyone with the link, and the S3 bucket is public.
truths: Origins should only accept CloudFront traffic.
derivation: Create a **key group** with public keys.
Use **OAC** so S3 only serves CloudFront.

analogy.title: Event tickets versus a wristband
analogy.story: A ticket admits you to one show; a wristband lets you into every stage at the festival.
analogy.breaks: Wristbands are hard to copy; cookies and URLs can be shared, so keep expiries short.

example.title: Member-only streaming
flow: User logs in → app sets signed cookies for /videos/123/*
Player fetches HLS segments with cookies

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Only paying users stream, links useless elsewhere.

check.q: When are signed cookies better than signed URLs?
check.a: When granting access to many files, such as video segments or a whole section, without changing URLs.

cache-behavior-and-cache-key-engineering.core: The cache key decides whether two requests share a cached object. Include only what changes the response (specific query strings, headers, cookies) via cache policies; forward extra values to the origin with origin request policies instead. Path-based cache behaviours apply different TTLs and policies per route. Over-broad keys destroy hit ratios.

first_principles.problem: Forwarding all headers and cookies makes every request unique, and the cache hit ratio is 5%.
truths: Origins may need data that doesn't affect the response.
Different paths have different freshness needs.
derivation: Use **origin request policies** for non-key data.

analogy.title: Labelling leftovers in a fridge
analogy.story: If every container is labelled with the time to the second, you never reuse anything.
analogy.breaks: Fridges spoil food; caches expire by TTL, not by smell.

example.title: Fixing the hit ratio
flow: Before: all headers + cookies in key → 5% hits
After: key = path + 'lang' query param; auth cookie forwarded only on /api/*
Static assets: 1-year TTL with hashed filenames

check.q: What's the difference between a cache policy and an origin request policy?
check.a: The cache policy defines the cache key (and TTLs); the origin request policy adds values sent to the origin without affecting the key.
